d: Every question here takes apart one sentence: "this signal (or coefficient) is statistically significant". The sentence can fail at several layers, and the sections follow those layers in order:

$$\begin{array}{ll} \textsf{Section} & \textsf{Question it answers} \\ \hline \textsf{Testing basics} & \textsf{what errors can one test make; is the effect worth anything} \\ \textsf{Multiple testing} & \textsf{after many tests, how much is "significant" worth} \\ \textsf{OLS assumptions} & \textsf{is the t-stat's standard error computed correctly} \\ \textsf{Regression pitfalls} & \textsf{does the coefficient measure what you think} \\ \textsf{Fit \& regularization} & \textsf{does a good fit mean good prediction} \\ \textsf{Asset pricing} & \textsf{is a slope a sensitivity or a premium; its SE} \\ \textsf{Forecast comparison} & \textsf{is one model really better than another} \end{array}$$
Each item below follows the same pattern: what it answers → definition → symbols → a worked example with numbers → key points.
The questions live in three different settings, so three examples are used. Each item says which one it uses.
Signal A (one return series, used for testing): a long-short signal with independent daily returns, true mean $\mu=3$ bp $=0.0003$, sd $\sigma=1\%$; daily turnover 10%, one-way cost 5 bp.

Regression P (time series, used for fit and standard errors): a standardized signal $x_t$ (mean 0, sd 1) predicts next month's market return: $$r_{t+1}=0.5\%+\beta x_t+u_{t+1},\quad \beta=0.5\%,\quad \mathrm{sd}(r_{t+1})=5\%$$ Population $R^2=\beta^2/\mathrm{Var}(r)=0.005^2/0.05^2=1\%$: real but weak. 20 years, $n=240$ months.

Research R (cross-section, used for regressions on stocks): $N=500$ stocks, $T=120$ months. New signal $S$, existing factor momentum $M$, target next-month return $Y$. Cross-sectional correlations (think ICs): $\rho_{SY}=0.04$, $\rho_{SM}=0.6$, $\rho_{MY}=0.05$.
Answers: when testing whether A's mean is 0, what can go wrong?

$$\begin{array}{lll} \textsf{Term} & \textsf{Meaning} & \textsf{Symbols} \\ \hline H_0 \textsf{ vs } H_1 & \theta\in\Theta_0 \textsf{ vs } \theta\in\Theta_1 & \theta = \textsf{unknown parameter} \\ \textsf{Rejection region} & \textsf{reject } H_0 \textsf{ if } T(X)>c & T = \textsf{statistic},\ c = \textsf{critical value} \\ \textsf{Type I error} & H_0 \textsf{ true, rejected} & \textsf{false positive} \\ \textsf{Type II error} & H_0 \textsf{ false, kept} & \textsf{false negative} \end{array}$$

Power function: $\beta(\theta)=P_\theta(X\in R)$, the probability of rejecting when the true parameter is $\theta$. On $\Theta_0$ it is the Type I error probability; on $\Theta_1$ it is the power. Size $=\sup_{\theta\in\Theta_0}\beta(\theta)$; a level-$\alpha$ test has size $\le\alpha$.
Key point: fixing $\alpha$ controls only Type I error. A larger rejection region lowers Type II error and raises Type I error.
Answers: with 5 years of A's data, what is the chance of detecting it?

Two-sided z-test of $H_0:\mu=0$ with true mean $\delta$, noise $\sigma$, $n$ observations: $$\text{power}=\Phi\Big(\frac{\delta\sqrt n}{\sigma}-z_{1-\alpha/2}\Big)+\Phi\Big(-\frac{\delta\sqrt n}{\sigma}-z_{1-\alpha/2}\Big)$$ The second term is tiny. For 80% power at 5%: $$n\approx\Big(\frac{(z_{0.975}+z_{0.8})\,\sigma}{\delta}\Big)^2=\Big(\frac{2.80\,\sigma}{\delta}\Big)^2$$
Symbols: $\delta/\sigma$ is the per-period Sharpe ratio; $z_{1-\alpha/2}=1.96$ at 5%; $\Phi$ the standard normal CDF.
Example (A): $\delta/\sigma=0.03$ a day, annual Sharpe $0.03\sqrt{252}=0.48$.

$$\begin{array}{lccc} \textsf{Data} & \textsf{n} & \delta\sqrt n/\sigma & \textsf{Power} \\ \hline 1\textsf{ year} & \textsf{252} & \textsf{0.48} & \textsf{7.6\%} \\ 5\textsf{ years} & \textsf{1260} & \textsf{1.06} & \textsf{18.7\%} \\ 10\textsf{ years} & \textsf{2520} & \textsf{1.51} & \textsf{32.5\%} \\ 20\textsf{ years} & \textsf{5040} & \textsf{2.13} & \textsf{56.7\%} \\ 34.6\textsf{ years} & \textsf{8721} & \textsf{2.80} & \textsf{80\%} \end{array}$$
Relationship: power depends on the data only through $\delta\sqrt n/\sigma$. Halve the Sharpe and you need four times the years. Most single signals are underpowered.
Answers: what does a p-value look like when there is nothing there? (Bridge to multiple testing.)
Definition: p-value $=P_{H_0}(|T|\ge|t_{\text{obs}}|)$, the probability, assuming $H_0$, of a statistic at least as extreme as the one observed. It is not the probability that $H_0$ is true.
Theorem: for a continuous statistic, under $H_0$ the p-value is Uniform(0,1). So "reject if $p<\alpha$" has Type I error exactly $\alpha$.
Key point: a histogram of many p-values is flat if all are noise; real effects pile up near 0.
Answers: the t-stat is fine. Is the effect big enough to trade?

Definition (Wooldridge): statistical significance is decided by $t=\hat\beta/\mathrm{se}(\hat\beta)$; economic significance by the size and sign of $\hat\beta$. A big $t$ can come from a tiny $\mathrm{se}$ (large sample), not a big effect.
Book example: 401(k) participation on firm size, coefficient $-0.00013$, $t=-3.25$. Yet 10,000 more employees lowers participation by only $10000\times0.00013=1.3$ points.
Example (A vs B): daily cost $=2\times\text{turnover}\times\text{one-way cost}$.

$$\begin{array}{lcccccc} \textsf{Signal} & \textsf{gross/day} & \textsf{vol} & \textsf{turnover} & \textsf{cost/day} & \textsf{net/yr} & \textsf{20-yr gross } t \\ \hline \textsf{A} & 3\textsf{ bp} & \textsf{1\%} & \textsf{10\%} & 1\textsf{ bp} & \textsf{5.04\%} & \textsf{2.13} \\ \textsf{B} & 1\textsf{ bp} & \textsf{0.2\%} & \textsf{20\%} & 2\textsf{ bp} & \textsf{-2.52\%} & \textsf{3.55} \end{array}$$
Relationship: B is more significant and loses money; A is less significant and earns a net Sharpe of 0.32. You need both: "is it zero?" and "is it worth it after costs?".
Answers: one test has Type I error $\alpha$. With 1,000 tests, what does "error" even mean?

$$\begin{array}{lccc}  & H_0\textsf{ true} & H_0\textsf{ false} & \textsf{Total} \\ \hline \textsf{Reject} & \textsf{V} & \textsf{S} & \textsf{R} \\ \textsf{Keep} & \textsf{U} & \textsf{W} & \textsf{m-R} \\ \hline \textsf{Total} & m_0 & m-m_0 & \textsf{m} \end{array}$$
Symbols: $V$ false positives, $S$ true positives, $W$ false negatives. All are random; only $R$ is observed.
FWER $=P(V\ge1)$. For $m$ independent true nulls each tested at $\alpha$: $\mathrm{FWER}=1-(1-\alpha)^m$.

$$\begin{array}{lcccc} \textsf{m} & \textsf{1} & \textsf{5} & \textsf{100} & \textsf{1000} \\ \hline \alpha=0.05 & \textsf{0.05} & \textsf{0.226} & \textsf{0.994} & \approx1 \\ \alpha=0.01 & \textsf{0.01} & \textsf{0.049} & \textsf{0.634} & \approx1 \end{array}$$
Book example: a broker sends 1,024 clients every possible 10-day up/down call; one client sees 10 correct calls by construction.

Bonferroni: reject only if $p_j<\alpha/m$. Proof by the union bound, no independence needed: $$\mathrm{FWER}=P\Big(\bigcup_j A_j\Big)\le\sum_j P(A_j)\le m\cdot\frac{\alpha}{m}=\alpha$$ $A_j$ = "null $j$ is true but rejected".
Holm (step-down): sort p-values; compare them in turn with $\alpha/m,\ \alpha/(m-1),\dots$; stop at the first failure. Also controls FWER, never rejects fewer than Bonferroni.

Book example (5 fund managers, p-values 0.006, 0.918, 0.012, 0.601, 0.756): uncorrected rejects One and Three; Bonferroni (0.01) rejects only One; Holm: $0.006<0.01$, $0.012<0.0125$, $0.601>0.0167$, rejects One and Three.
Key point: Bonferroni is valid under any dependence but conservative, paid for in Type II errors.
Answers: if a few false positives are acceptable, how do you get more discoveries?
FDP $=V/R$ (0 if $R=0$), the false share among this sample's rejections; FDR $=E(\text{FDP})$.
BH at level $q$: sort $p_{(1)}\le\dots\le p_{(m)}$; $L=\max\{j:\ p_{(j)}<qj/m\}$; reject all with $p\le p_{(L)}$. Then $\mathrm{FDR}\le\frac{m_0}{m}q\le q$ (independent or mildly dependent p-values).
Example (10 tests, $q=0.05$):

$$\begin{array}{lcccccc} \textsf{j} & \textsf{1} & \textsf{2} & \textsf{3} & \textsf{4} & \textsf{5} & \textsf{6} \\ \hline p_{(j)} & \textsf{0.00017} & \textsf{0.00448} & \textsf{0.00671} & \textsf{0.00907} & \textsf{0.01220} & \textsf{0.33626} \\ \textsf{BH line } 0.05j/10 & \textsf{0.005} & \textsf{0.010} & \textsf{0.015} & \textsf{0.020} & \textsf{0.025} & \textsf{0.030} \end{array}$$ Bonferroni (0.005) rejects 2; BH rejects 5.

Example (A, simulated): 900 noise signals + 100 like A. With 5 years, uncorrected FDR is 0.71 and BH finds 0.16 of the 100 real ones; with 20 years BH finds 9.1. The bottleneck is power, not the correction.
Key point: there is no standard FDR level like 5%: smaller when follow-up is expensive, larger when cheap.
Answers: R's new signal shows $t=3$. Does that survive the number of tries?
One pre-specified test: $p=2[1-\Phi(3)]=0.0027$. With $m$ independent null tries: $P(\text{some }|t|\ge3)=1-(1-0.0027)^m$.

$$\begin{array}{lccccc} \textsf{m} & \textsf{1} & \textsf{10} & \textsf{50} & \textsf{100} & \textsf{200} \\ \hline P(\textsf{some }|t|\ge3) & \textsf{0.27\%} & \textsf{2.7\%} & \textsf{12.6\%} & \textsf{23.7\%} & \textsf{41.8\%} \\ \textsf{Bonferroni bar} & \textsf{1.96} & \textsf{2.81} & \textsf{3.29} & \textsf{3.48} & \textsf{3.66} \end{array}$$
Bar: $t^*=\Phi^{-1}(1-\alpha/(2M))$. Using about 316 published factors, the bar is 3.78. The hard part is $M$: variants others tried and reports you read also count.

Checklist before believing it: number of variants; timestamps, restatements, survivorship; stability across subsamples, sectors, small parameter changes; what is left after neutralizing size, industry, momentum; costs and capacity; overlapping returns. Then replicate on untouched data.
Answers: the t-stats above assumed the regression is right. Which assumptions give an unbiased coefficient?

MLR.1 linear in parameters: $y=\beta_0+\beta_1x_1+\dots+\beta_kx_k+u$. MLR.2 random sampling. MLR.3 no perfect collinearity (no exact linear relation among regressors, none constant). MLR.4 zero conditional mean: $E(u\mid x_1,\dots,x_k)=0$.
Symbols: $y$ e.g. next month's return; $x_j$ e.g. signal, size; $\beta_j$ unknown constants; $u$ everything not in the model (random).

Theorem 3.1: under MLR.1–4, $E(\hat\beta_j)=\beta_j$. Matrix proof: $$\hat\beta=(X'X)^{-1}X'y=\beta+(X'X)^{-1}X'u,\qquad E(\hat\beta\mid X)=\beta$$ using $E(u\mid X)=0$ for the whole matrix $X$ (strict exogeneity in time series).

Key points: MLR.3 allows correlated regressors, only not perfectly. MLR.4 is the one that breaks (omitted variables, measurement error, simultaneity, look-ahead) and can never be checked from the data. Unbiasedness is a property of the procedure, not of one estimate.

MLR.5 homoskedasticity: $\mathrm{Var}(u\mid x)=\sigma^2$. MLR.1–5 = Gauss-Markov ⇒ OLS is BLUE and (Theorem 3.2) $$\mathrm{Var}(\hat\beta_j)=\frac{\sigma^2}{\mathrm{SST}_j(1-R_j^2)},\qquad \mathrm{SST}_j=\sum_i(x_{ij}-\bar x_j)^2$$ $R_j^2$ = $R^2$ from regressing $x_j$ on the other regressors.
MLR.6 normality: $u\sim N(0,\sigma^2)$ independent of $x$. MLR.1–6 = classical linear model ⇒ $(\hat\beta_j-\beta_j)/\mathrm{se}(\hat\beta_j)\sim t_{n-k-1}$ exactly.
Large samples (Theorem 5.2): MLR.1–5 alone give an asymptotically normal $t$; normality is not needed. Homoskedasticity still is.

$$\begin{array}{ll} \textsf{Assumptions} & \textsf{What you get} \\ \hline \textsf{MLR.1--4} & \textsf{unbiased } \hat\beta \\ \textsf{+ MLR.5} & \textsf{usual SE formula, BLUE} \\ \textsf{+ MLR.6} & \textsf{exact } t \textsf{ in small samples} \\ \textsf{MLR.1--5, large } n & \textsf{approx. normal } t \end{array}$$
Example (R-like): 3,000 stocks, $x_1$ variance 1, correlation 0.6 with $x_2$ ($R_1^2=0.36$), error sd 10%: $\mathrm{sd}(\hat\beta_1)=0.10/\sqrt{3000\times0.64}=0.228\%$.
Answers: what if error variance differs across observations (small caps noisier than large caps)?
Definition: $\mathrm{Var}(u_i\mid x_i)=\sigma_i^2$ varies with $i$.
Unchanged: unbiasedness, consistency, $R^2$. Changed: usual SEs and $t$, $F$ tests are wrong, and large samples do not fix it; OLS is no longer BLUE.

True variance, simple regression: $$\mathrm{Var}(\hat\beta_1)=\frac{\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2\sigma_i^2}{\mathrm{SST}_x^2}$$ White's estimator plugs in $\hat u_i^2$ for $\sigma_i^2$. Points far from $\bar x$ get more weight.

Example (P cross-section, simulated): 500 stocks, $\mathrm{Var}(u\mid x)\propto0.2+x^2$, true $\beta=0$. Usual SE is too small by $\sqrt{E[x^2(0.2+x^2)]/E(0.2+x^2)}=\sqrt{3.2/1.2}=1.63$×; a nominal 5% test rejects 22.6% of the time with usual SEs, 5.5% with White.
WLS: if $\mathrm{Var}(u\mid x)=\sigma^2h(x)$ with $h$ known, divide the equation by $\sqrt{h_i}$ and run OLS (more efficient). Robust SEs need no $h$.
Answers: in time series, errors in different periods are correlated. What happens to the SE?

AR(1) errors $u_t=\rho u_{t-1}+e_t$, $\bar x=0$: $$\mathrm{Var}(\hat\beta_1)=\frac{\sigma^2}{\mathrm{SST}_x}+\frac{2\sigma^2}{\mathrm{SST}_x^2}\sum_{t=1}^{n-1}\sum_{j=1}^{n-t}\rho^jx_tx_{t+j}$$ The usual formula keeps only the first term. With strict exogeneity $\hat\beta$ stays unbiased.
When it matters: both $x$ and $u$ must be autocorrelated. Long-sample variance inflation $\approx(1+\rho_x\rho_u)/(1-\rho_x\rho_u)$:

$$\begin{array}{lcc} (\rho_x,\rho_u) & \textsf{Var inflation} & \textsf{SE inflation} \\ \hline (0.95,\,0) & \textsf{1.00} & \textsf{1.00} \\ (0.5,\,0.5) & \textsf{1.67} & \textsf{1.29} \\ (0.9,\,0.9) & \textsf{9.53} & \textsf{3.09} \end{array}$$

Newey-West: with $\hat a_t=\hat r_t\hat u_t$ ($\hat r_t$ = residual of $x_1$ on the other regressors), $$\hat\nu=\sum_t\hat a_t^2+2\sum_{h=1}^{g}\Big(1-\frac{h}{g+1}\Big)\sum_{t>h}\hat a_t\hat a_{t-h}$$ Bartlett weights keep $\hat\nu\ge0$; $g$ = lags allowed (rule of thumb $\lfloor4(n/100)^{2/9}\rfloor$; at least $h-1$ for $h$-period overlapping returns).

Example (P with 12-month overlapping returns, persistent $x$, true $\beta=0$, simulated): false rejection at 5% is 54.6% with usual SEs, 56.3% White, 16.8% Newey-West $g=12$, 4.8% using only 20 non-overlapping years.
Key point: NW helps but still over-rejects with persistent regressors and $n$ around 100–240. The non-overlapping test has the right size but low power.
Answers: MLR.4 is the assumption that governs bias. What is the commonest way it breaks, and in which direction?

True model $y=\beta_0+\beta_1x_1+\beta_2x_2+u$; you regress $y$ on $x_1$ only: $$E(\tilde\beta_1)=\beta_1+\beta_2\tilde\delta_1,\qquad \tilde\delta_1=\frac{\widehat{\mathrm{Cov}}(x_1,x_2)}{\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(x_1)}$$
Symbols: $\tilde\beta_1$ short-regression slope; $\beta_2$ true effect of the omitted $x_2$; $\tilde\delta_1$ slope of $x_2$ on $x_1$.
$$\begin{array}{lcc}  & \mathrm{Corr}(x_1,x_2)>0 & \mathrm{Corr}(x_1,x_2)<0 \\ \hline \beta_2>0 & \textsf{upward} & \textsf{downward} \\ \beta_2<0 & \textsf{downward} & \textsf{upward} \end{array}$$

Example (simulated): $x_1$ = low analyst coverage, $x_2$ = smallness, correlation 0.6; truth $\beta_1=0$, $\beta_2=0.3\%$/month. Short regression gives $0.6\times0.3\%=0.18\%$/month; averaged over 240 months its $t\approx15$. The more significant, the easier it is to mistake bias for alpha.

Over-controlling: do not control for the channel the signal works through. If the signal acts only via liquidity, controlling for liquidity removes the effect (0.205% → 0.012% in simulation). Confounders: control. Mediators: don't. Telling them apart needs economics, not statistics.
Answers: $S$ has IC 0.04. How much of it is borrowed from momentum?

Frisch-Waugh: in $y=\beta_0+\beta_1x_1+\beta_2x_2+u$, $$\hat\beta_1=\frac{\sum_i\hat r_{i1}y_i}{\sum_i\hat r_{i1}^2}$$ $\hat r_{i1}$ = residual of $x_1$ regressed on $x_2$. "Controlling for $x_2$" means removing from $x_1$ the part $x_2$ explains.
Simple vs multiple slope: $\tilde\beta_1=\hat\beta_1+\hat\beta_2\tilde\delta_1$. Example (R, standardized): $0.04=0.0156+0.0406\times0.6$: 0.0244 of the raw IC is momentum's effect times the overlap.
Partial correlation: correlate the residuals of both $X$ and $Y$ on $Z$. One control: $$\rho_{XY\cdot Z}=\frac{\rho_{XY}-\rho_{XZ}\rho_{YZ}}{\sqrt{(1-\rho_{XZ}^2)(1-\rho_{YZ}^2)}}$$

$$\begin{array}{lc} \textsf{Quantity (R)} & \textsf{Value} \\ \hline \rho_{SY} \textsf{ (raw IC)} & \textsf{0.0400} \\ \textsf{via momentum } \rho_{SM}\rho_{MY} & \textsf{0.0300} \\ \textsf{numerator} & \textsf{0.0100} \\ \textsf{denominator } \sqrt{0.64\times0.9975} & \textsf{0.7990} \\ \rho_{SY\cdot M} & \textsf{0.0125} \end{array}$$

Key points: same numerator as the multiple-regression coefficient, so the two tests agree. Removes only linear effects of the controls included; says nothing about causality or costs. "Neutralize, then compute IC" is a partial correlation.
Answers: why is a coefficient imprecise when regressors are correlated, while predictions are fine?

$$\mathrm{Var}(\hat\beta_j)=\frac{\sigma^2}{\mathrm{SST}_j}\cdot\mathrm{VIF}_j,\qquad \mathrm{VIF}_j=\frac{1}{1-R_j^2}$$ Three drivers: more noise $\sigma^2$, less variation $\mathrm{SST}_j$, more overlap $R_j^2$.

$$\begin{array}{lccccc} R_j^2 & \textsf{0} & \textsf{0.81} & \textsf{0.90} & \textsf{0.95} & \textsf{0.98} \\ \hline \mathrm{VIF} & \textsf{1} & \textsf{5.26} & \textsf{10} & \textsf{20} & \textsf{50} \end{array}$$ R: $S$ and $M$ correlate 0.6, VIF 1.56, SE ×1.25.
Why prediction survives (simulated, correlation 0.95, $n=100$, $\beta_1=\beta_2=1$): the RSS surface is a long valley along $\beta_1-\beta_2$.

$$\begin{array}{lc} \textsf{Quantity} & \textsf{sd} \\ \hline \hat\beta_1 & \textsf{0.329} \\ \hat\beta_1+\hat\beta_2 & \textsf{0.102} \\ \textsf{prediction, same structure} & \textsf{0.177} \\ \textsf{prediction at } x=(1,-1) & \textsf{0.657} \end{array}$$

Key points: high collinearity violates no assumption and OLS stays unbiased; VIF cut-offs (5, 10) are arbitrary. Danger comes when new data move along the valley (features decouple). Fixes: drop one, average the group, ridge, PCA.
Answers: P's in-sample $R^2$ goes from 1% to 17% after adding 19 features. Which model is better?

$$R^2=1-\frac{\mathrm{RSS}}{\mathrm{TSS}},\qquad \bar R^2=1-(1-R^2)\frac{n-1}{n-k-1}$$ RSS = $\sum(y_i-\hat y_i)^2$, TSS = $\sum(y_i-\bar y)^2$. $R^2$ never falls when a variable is added (the old solution is still available). $\bar R^2$ rises iff the new variable has $|t|>1$, and can be negative.
Under pure noise with $k$ features: $E(R^2)=k/(n-1)$.

$$\begin{array}{lccc} \textsf{n} & \textsf{k} & E(R^2) & \textsf{simulated} \\ \hline \textsf{240} & \textsf{20} & \textsf{0.0837} & \textsf{0.0837} \\ \textsf{120} & \textsf{20} & \textsf{0.168} & \textsf{0.167} \end{array}$$
Key point: a low $R^2$ does not mean biased coefficients; a high in-sample $R^2$ does not mean prediction.

$$R^2_{\text{OOS}}=1-\frac{\sum_{t\in\text{test}}(y_t-\hat y_t)^2}{\sum_{t\in\text{test}}(y_t-\bar y_{\text{train}})^2}$$ $\hat y_t$ uses only data before the test period; the benchmark is the training mean. Negative = worse than the historical mean.
Example (P, train 120 months, test 120, simulated):

$$\begin{array}{lccc} \textsf{Model} & \textsf{in-sample } R^2 & R^2_{\textsf{OOS}} & \textsf{share} >0 \\ \hline x_t \textsf{ only} & \textsf{1.75\%} & \textsf{0.19\%} & \textsf{58\%} \\ x_t + 19 \textsf{ noise} & \textsf{17.4\%} & \textsf{-19.4\%} & \textsf{2\%} \\ 20 \textsf{ noise} & \textsf{16.7\%} & \textsf{-20.5\%} & \textsf{1\%} \end{array}$$
Relationship: in-sample and OOS move in opposite directions. Even the true model is negative OOS 42% of the time: with population $R^2=1\%$ and 120 months, estimation error is as large as the signal.
With one linear predictor $R^2=IC^2$. Fundamental law: $IR\approx IC\sqrt{BR}$, $BR$ = independent bets per year.

$$\begin{array}{lcccc} \textsf{Setting} & \textsf{IC} & R^2 & \textsf{BR} & \textsf{IR} \\ \hline \textsf{market timing, quarterly} & \textsf{0.25} & \textsf{6.25\%} & \textsf{4} & \textsf{0.50} \\ \textsf{100 stocks, quarterly} & \textsf{0.025} & \textsf{0.06\%} & \textsf{400} & \textsf{0.50} \\ \textsf{P, monthly timing} & \textsf{0.10} & \textsf{1\%} & \textsf{12} & \textsf{0.35} \\ \textsf{500 stocks, monthly} & \textsf{0.05} & \textsf{0.25\%} & \textsf{6000} & \textsf{3.87} \end{array}$$
Key point: stock selection with a tiny $R^2$ can match timing with a large one, through breadth. Bets on the same day share factors, so the last row is an upper bound.
Answers: where does P's −19% OOS come from, and how to cut it?

$$E\big(y_0-\hat f(x_0)\big)^2=\mathrm{Var}\big(\hat f(x_0)\big)+\mathrm{Bias}\big(\hat f(x_0)\big)^2+\mathrm{Var}(\epsilon)$$ Expectation over training sets and the new point. In P, $\mathrm{Var}(\epsilon)$ is 99% of the variance; OLS with 20 features on 120 months adds a variance term of about 17–20% of TSS.

Ridge: $\min\ \mathrm{RSS}+\lambda\sum_j\beta_j^2$, solution $(X'X+\lambda I)^{-1}X'y$ (features standardized, intercept not penalized). Along an eigen-direction of $X'X/n$ with eigenvalue $d$ it keeps $d/(d+\lambda)$ of the OLS coefficient. Two features with correlation 0.95: eigenvalues 1.95 (sum) and 0.05 (difference).

$$\begin{array}{lccc} \lambda & \textsf{kept, sum} & \textsf{kept, difference} & \textsf{condition no.} \\ \hline \textsf{0} & \textsf{100\%} & \textsf{100\%} & \textsf{39} \\ \textsf{0.1} & \textsf{95\%} & \textsf{33\%} & \textsf{13.7} \\ \textsf{1} & \textsf{66\%} & \textsf{5\%} & \textsf{2.8} \end{array}$$
Lasso: $\min\ \mathrm{RSS}+\lambda\sum_j|\beta_j|$. Orthonormal case, $\lambda=0.5$: ridge divides by 1.5, lasso subtracts 0.25 and zeroes the rest.

$$\begin{array}{lcc} \textsf{OLS} & \textsf{ridge} & \textsf{lasso} \\ \hline \textsf{0.8} & \textsf{0.533} & \textsf{0.55} \\ \textsf{0.3} & \textsf{0.200} & \textsf{0.05} \\ \textsf{-0.2} & \textsf{-0.133} & \textsf{0} \end{array}$$

Example (P with 20 correlated features, $\lambda$ by expanding-window CV, simulated): mean $R^2_{\text{OOS}}$ OLS −18.7%, ridge −0.07%, lasso −0.04%. Regularization removes the variance term; it cannot create signal.

Leakage: choose $\lambda$ and standardization inside the training period only; with overlapping labels, purge training points whose label window reaches the validation period, and add an embargo after it.
Answers: how do you get a standard error for a statistic with no formula (Sharpe ratio), and when does that fail?

Empirical distribution $\hat F_n$ puts mass $1/n$ on each data point. Bootstrap: $V_F(T_n)\approx V_{\hat F_n}(T_n)\approx v_{\text{boot}}$. Draw $n$ points with replacement, recompute $T_n^*$, repeat $B$ times, take the variance.

Example (P's 240 i.i.d. months): SE of the mean, formula 0.325% vs bootstrap 0.329%; SE of the annual Sharpe, true 0.226 vs bootstrap 0.228. The 95% interval for a Sharpe of 0.35 is about $[-0.09,0.80]$: still contains 0 after 20 years.
Failure: $\hat F_n$ assumes i.i.d. With AR(1) returns, $\rho=0.5$: $$\mathrm{SD}(\bar X)\approx\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}\sqrt{\frac{1+\rho}{1-\rho}}=0.323\%\times\sqrt3=0.559\%$$

$$\begin{array}{lcc} \textsf{Method (simulated)} & \textsf{SE} & \textsf{share of truth} \\ \hline \textsf{naive (block 1)} & \textsf{0.320\%} & \textsf{57\%} \\ \textsf{block } 6 & \textsf{0.483\%} & \textsf{86\%} \\ \textsf{block } 12 & \textsf{0.507\%} & \textsf{91\%} \end{array}$$
Key point: moving-block bootstrap keeps dependence inside blocks (start near $n^{1/3}$); for panels resample whole dates.
Answers: the same $N\times T$ panel can be regressed in two directions. What does each slope mean?
Time series (fix stock $i$): $r_{it}=\alpha_i+\beta_if_t+\epsilon_{it}$. $\beta_i$ = exposure, $\alpha_i$ = pricing error when $f_t$ is a traded return.
Cross-section (fix date $t$): $r_{it}=\gamma_{0t}+\lambda_tz_{it}+u_{it}$. $z_{it}$ = characteristic known at the start of the period; $\lambda_t$ = premium earned per unit of $z$ this period.
The cross-sectional slope is a portfolio return: $$\hat\lambda_t=\sum_iw_{it}r_{it},\qquad w_{it}=\frac{z_{it}-\bar z_t}{\sum_j(z_{jt}-\bar z_t)^2},\qquad \sum_iw_{it}=0,\ \sum_iw_{it}z_{it}=1$$

$$\begin{array}{lll}  & \textsf{Time series} & \textsf{Cross-section} \\ \hline \textsf{Fixed} & \textsf{stock } i & \textsf{date } t \\ \textsf{Slope} & \beta_i\textsf{: sensitivity} & \lambda_t\textsf{: premium} \\ \textsf{Intercept} & \alpha_i\textsf{: pricing error} & \gamma_{0t}\textsf{: common part} \\ \textsf{Use} & \textsf{exposure, attribution} & \textsf{alpha research} \end{array}$$
Answers: we have $T$ estimates $\hat\lambda_t$. Is the average premium nonzero, and what is its SE?
$$\bar\lambda=\frac1T\sum_t\hat\lambda_t,\qquad \mathrm{se}(\bar\lambda)=\frac{s_\lambda}{\sqrt T}$$ Example (R): $\bar\lambda=0.40\%$, $s_\lambda=1.5\%$, $T=120$: se 0.137%, $t=2.92$.

Why not pooled OLS: a common shock hits every stock in a month ($\lambda_t=\lambda+\eta_t$). Pooled OLS treats $N\times T$ points as independent; FM puts each month's shock into one $\hat\lambda_t$, so it enters $s_\lambda$. Simulated ($N=500$, $T=120$): FM se 0.156%, $t=2.57$; pooled se 0.045%, $t=9.05$. Under a zero premium, pooled rejects 41% at 5%, FM 5.6%.

Autocorrelated $\hat\lambda_t$: $\mathrm{Var}(\bar\lambda)$ gains $2\sum_k(1-k/T)\rho_k$. AR(1) with $\phi=0.3$: inflation $1.3/0.7=1.857$, se $0.137\%\to0.187\%$, $t$ $2.92\to2.14$. Use Newey-West on $\hat\lambda_t-\bar\lambda$.

Errors-in-variables: if $z$ is an estimated beta, $$\mathrm{plim}\,\hat\lambda=\lambda\cdot\frac{\sigma^2_{z^*}}{\sigma^2_{z^*}+\sigma^2_e}$$ e.g. $0.09/(0.09+0.04)=0.69$: premium understated by 31%. Fixes: portfolio betas, Shanken correction for the SE. Persistent firm effects: cluster by firm.
Answers: "which model is better" means nothing until the loss is fixed.
Forecast $f_t$ of $y_{t+1}$ from information $I_t$; error $e_{t+1}=y_{t+1}-f_t$. Under squared loss the best forecast is $E(y_{t+1}\mid I_t)$.
$$\mathrm{RMSE}=\Big(\frac1m\sum e^2\Big)^{1/2},\qquad \mathrm{MAE}=\frac1m\sum|e|$$ over $m$ OOS points. In quant work the loss can also be rank IC or portfolio P&L.
Book example: unemployment, 7 OOS years: AR(1) RMSE 0.962 vs VAR(1) 0.673. Whether that gap is real with $m=7$ is the question DM answers.

$$d_t=L(e_{A,t})-L(e_{B,t}),\qquad DM=\frac{\bar d}{\sqrt{\widehat{\mathrm{LRV}}(d)/m}}\ \to N(0,1)$$ LRV = long-run variance via Newey-West; $h$-step forecasts make $d_t$ MA($h-1$), so use at least $h-1$ lags.
Example (simulated): truth $y=0.5x+u$; A forecasts $0.5x$, B $0.3x$; $m=120$.

$$\begin{array}{lc} \textsf{Quantity} & \textsf{Value} \\ \hline \textsf{MSE A / MSE B, one sample} & 1.1642 / 1.1627 \\ \textsf{corr of the two squared-error series} & \textsf{0.97} \\ \textsf{power, paired DM} & \textsf{21\%} \\ \textsf{power, unpaired test} & \textsf{0\%} \\ m \textsf{ for 80\% power} & \approx800 \end{array}$$
Relationship: both errors share the same $y_t$, so pairing removes the common part and makes the test far more powerful; even so, small true differences need long samples.
Key points: nested models → Clark-West; tuning inside the rolling window; many models → model confidence set, reality check / SPA. In practice: NW $t$-test on the difference of two IC series.
Casella-Berger use $\beta(\theta)$ for the power function; many texts use $\beta$ for the Type II error probability (power $=1-\beta$). Opposite meanings: say which.

Wooldridge: SSR = residual sum of squares, SST = total. ISL: RSS and TSS for the same things. $\mathrm{SST}_j$ (one regressor's variation) and $R_j^2$ (regressor on regressors) are not the $y$-regression quantities.
Ridge/lasso penalty vs cross-sectional factor premium $\lambda_t$. Unrelated.

The reference answer to Q27 says residual autocorrelation with lagged $y$ regressors makes OLS inconsistent. Too broad: if $E(u_t\mid y_{t-1})=0$, OLS is consistent and only the SEs are wrong; inconsistency needs AR errors on top, and then $y_t$ is really AR(2).

cards.q: A two-sided z-test at level $\alpha$ checks whether a mean equals 0; the true effect is $\delta$, noise sd $\sigma$, $n$ observations. (1) Define Type I error, Type II error and power. (2) Write the approximate power. (3) What raises power at fixed $\alpha$? (4) What $n$ gives 80% power at 5%, and what does that mean for a strategy with annual Sharpe 0.5?
pts: (1) Type I: reject a true null (false positive), probability $\le\alpha$. Type II: fail to reject a false null (false negative), probability $\beta$. Power $=1-\beta$.
(2) $$\text{power}\approx\Phi\Big(\frac{\delta\sqrt n}{\sigma}-z_{1-\alpha/2}\Big)$$
(3) Larger $\delta$, larger $n$, smaller $\sigma$. Lowering $\alpha$ lowers power.

(4) $n\approx\big((z_{0.975}+z_{0.8})\sigma/\delta\big)^2=(2.8\,\sigma/\delta)^2$. Annual Sharpe 0.5: $(2.8/0.5)^2\approx31$ years. Single weak signals are underpowered; lean on breadth, priors and OOS checks.

cards.q: (1) What question does statistical significance answer, and what does economic significance answer? (2) Why can a tiny effect be significant? Use 1 bp a day, 0.2% daily vol, 20 years. (3) Same signal turns over 20% of the book a day at 5 bp per side: is it worth trading? (4) What would you look at besides the t-stat?
pts: (1) Statistical: could the effect be zero? ($t$ = estimate / SE). Economic: is it big enough to matter after costs? (the size of the estimate).
(2) SE shrinks like $1/\sqrt n$: $t=\frac{0.01\%}{0.2\%}\sqrt{5040}\approx3.5$.
(3) Cost $=0.2\times2\times5$ bp $=2$ bp a day > 1 bp gross: net negative.
(4) Effect size, turnover and net returns, capacity, drawdowns, correlation with existing factors. A signal must be both real and worth trading.

cards.q: You test 1,000 candidate signals and 50 have p-values below 5%. (1) What would pure noise produce? (2) What diagnostic would you look at first? (3) Which corrections apply, and what do they control? (4) What must survivors still pass?
pts: (1) Under the null p-values are $U(0,1)$: expect $1000\times5\%=50$, sd $\sqrt{1000\cdot0.05\cdot0.95}\approx6.9$. 50 is exactly the noise level.
(2) The p-value histogram: flat means noise; a spike near 0 means some real signals.
(3) Bonferroni ($p<0.05/1000$) controls the family-wise error rate; Benjamini-Hochberg controls the false discovery rate and is more powerful.
(4) OOS tests, an economic story, subperiod stability, and not being fifty variants of one factor.

cards.q: $m$ hypotheses are tested with p-values $p_{(1)}\le\dots\le p_{(m)}$. (1) Define FWER and FDR. (2) Give the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure at level $q$. (3) When do you prefer Bonferroni and when BH? (4) What is special about factor research?
pts: (1) FWER $=P(\text{at least one false rejection})$. FDR $=E[V/R]$, false rejections over all rejections (0 if none).
(2) Find the largest $k$ with $p_{(k)}\le\frac{k}{m}q$ and reject hypotheses $1,\dots,k$. FDR $\le q$ under independence (or positive dependence).
(3) Bonferroni when a single false positive is costly; BH when building a pool where a known share of false discoveries is acceptable.
(4) Signals are correlated variants, so tests are dependent and the real number of trials is unclear: record every trial, and expect Bonferroni to be conservative.

cards.q: A predictor has $t=3$ in your backtest. (1) What p-value does that mean for one pre-specified test? (2) What if you searched over 100 independent null signals? (3) List other reasons to reject it. (4) How would you get convincing evidence?
pts: (1) Two-sided $p\approx0.0027$.
(2) $P(\text{some }|t|\ge3)=1-(1-0.0027)^{100}\approx0.24$. Bonferroni for 100 tests at 5% needs $|t|\gtrsim3.5$.

(3) Leakage (point-in-time, restatements, survivorship); unstable across subperiods, sectors or small parameter changes; a known factor in disguise (size, industry, momentum); costs and capacity; overlapping returns inflating $t$.
(4) Pre-specify the test, count all trials, and replicate on untouched data (a new period or market), not more tuning on the same sample.

cards.q: Linear model $y=X\beta+u$. (1) Which assumptions make OLS unbiased? (2) Which extra assumption does the usual variance formula need? (3) Which does the exact t distribution need, and what changes in large samples? (4) What do you do in finance, and which assumption usually fails?
pts: (1) Linear in parameters, random sampling, no perfect collinearity ($X^\top X$ invertible), and zero conditional mean $E(u\mid X)=0$.
(2) Homoskedastic, serially uncorrelated errors: then $\mathrm{Var}(\hat\beta\mid X)=\sigma^2(X^\top X)^{-1}$ and OLS is BLUE (Gauss-Markov).
(3) Normal errors for exact $t$/$F$ in small samples. In large samples the CLT removes the need for normality, but not for (2).
(4) White or Newey-West standard errors. $E(u\mid X)=0$ is what usually fails: omitted factors and look-ahead bias.

cards.q: Simple regression $y=\beta_0+\beta_1x+u$ with $\mathrm{Var}(u_i\mid x)=\sigma_i^2$ varying across observations. (1) Is OLS biased? (2) What is the true variance of $\hat\beta_1$, and what goes wrong? (3) How do you fix inference?
pts: (1) No: unbiasedness only uses $E(u\mid x)=0$; the variance never enters that proof.

(2) $$\mathrm{Var}(\hat\beta_1\mid x)=\frac{\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2\sigma_i^2}{SST_x^2}$$ The usual $\sigma^2/SST_x$ is wrong even in large samples, so $t$ and $F$ tests are invalid; OLS is no longer BLUE.
(3) White robust SEs (plug in $\hat u_i^2$ for $\sigma_i^2$), or WLS if you trust a model for the variance.

cards.q: Time-series regression $y_t=\beta_0+\beta_1x_t+u_t$ with $\mathrm{Corr}(u_t,u_{t-k})\ne0$. (1) Where does residual autocorrelation come from? (2) Is OLS biased, and what happens to the usual SE? (3) How do you fix it? (4) What caveat remains?
pts: (1) Omitted dynamics, overlapping return horizons, omitted persistent state variables.
(2) Unbiased under strict exogeneity, but the usual SE drops the cross terms $\sum_t\sum_j\rho^j x_tx_{t+j}$. With both $x$ and $u$ positively autocorrelated it is far too small.
(3) Newey-West (HAC) SEs with lag at least the overlap; non-overlapping data; or model the dynamics.
(4) Newey-West still over-rejects in small samples with very persistent regressors: also check non-overlapping or simulation-based p-values.

cards.q: True model $y=\beta_0+\beta_1x_1+\beta_2x_2+u$, but you regress $y$ on $x_1$ only. (1) What does the slope converge to? (2) When is there no bias? (3) Give a cross-sectional return example. (4) How do you fix it, and what is the risk of the fix?
pts: (1) $$\tilde\beta_1\to\beta_1+\beta_2\,\frac{\mathrm{Cov}(x_1,x_2)}{\mathrm{Var}(x_1)}$$
(2) Bias needs both: $x_2$ matters for $y$ ($\beta_2\ne0$) and $x_2$ is correlated with $x_1$. Sign = sign($\beta_2$) × sign(correlation).
(3) "Low analyst coverage" predicts higher returns, but low-coverage stocks are small caps and size earns a premium: part of the alpha is size exposure. A large $t$ does not fix this.
(4) Control for or neutralise size, sector, beta. Do not over-control: if the signal works through liquidity, controlling for liquidity removes the real effect.

cards.q: (1) Define correlation and partial correlation. (2) Give the formula with one control $z$. (3) A new signal has IC 0.04, correlation 0.6 with momentum, and momentum has IC 0.05: what is its IC net of momentum? (4) What does partial correlation not tell you?
pts: (1) Correlation: linear co-movement. Partial: regress both variables on the controls and correlate the residuals (Frisch-Waugh).
(2) $$\rho_{xy\cdot z}=\frac{\rho_{xy}-\rho_{xz}\rho_{yz}}{\sqrt{(1-\rho_{xz}^2)(1-\rho_{yz}^2)}}$$
(3) $\frac{0.04-0.6\times0.05}{\sqrt{0.64\times0.9975}}\approx0.0125$: most of the 0.04 was momentum.
(4) It removes only linear effects of the controls you chose; it says nothing about causality or whether the residual signal survives costs.

cards.q: OLS under Gauss-Markov; $R_j^2$ is from regressing $x_j$ on the other regressors and $SST_j=\sum_i(x_{ij}-\bar x_j)^2$. (1) Write $\mathrm{Var}(\hat\beta_j)$ and the VIF. (2) Compute the VIF when two regressors have correlation 0.95. (3) Why can predictions still be fine? (4) When does it bite, and what are the fixes?
pts: (1) $$\mathrm{Var}(\hat\beta_j)=\frac{\sigma^2}{SST_j\,(1-R_j^2)},\qquad \mathrm{VIF}_j=\frac{1}{1-R_j^2}$$

(3) The data pin down $\beta_1+\beta_2$ but not the split: many coefficient pairs give nearly the same fitted values (a long valley in the RSS). Fine as long as new data keep the same collinear structure.
(4) Out of sample, when the features decouple. Fixes: ridge, PCA or averaging the group into one feature, and interpret only the group coefficient.

cards.q: (1) Why is in-sample $R^2$ a weak guide? Give its value under pure noise for 20 features and 240 months. (2) What should you use instead? (3) Why can a tiny $R^2$ still be valuable? (4) What do you judge a return model by?
pts: (1) $R^2$ never falls when regressors are added; under pure noise $E[R^2]\approx k/(n-1)=20/239\approx8\%$.
(2) Out-of-sample $R^2$ against the historical-mean forecast: $$R^2_{OOS}=1-\frac{\sum_t(r_t-\hat r_t)^2}{\sum_t(r_t-\bar r_t)^2}$$ It can be negative.

(3) For one linear signal $R^2=IC^2$: IC 0.05 is $R^2=0.25\%$. Fundamental law $IR\approx IC\sqrt{BR}$: 500 stocks monthly, $BR=6000$, theoretical IR $\approx3.9$ (less in practice: bets are correlated, costs).
(4) OOS $R^2$, IC and the net-of-cost Sharpe, not in-sample fit.

cards.q: (1) Write the ridge and lasso objectives. (2) Why do they help in return prediction? (3) How do they treat correlated features? (4) What leakage risk comes with them?
pts: (1) Ridge: $\min_\beta \lVert y-X\beta\rVert^2+\lambda\sum_j\beta_j^2$. Lasso: $+\lambda\sum_j|\beta_j|$.

(2) They trade a little bias for a large cut in variance; with a tiny signal-to-noise ratio, variance is the dominant error. OLS with many features often has negative OOS $R^2$; shrinkage brings it back near zero or slightly positive.
(3) Ridge spreads weight across correlated features; lasso sets some coefficients exactly to 0 (selection), picking somewhat arbitrarily within a correlated group.
(4) $\lambda$ and the standardisation must be fit on training folds only, with purging if labels overlap.

cards.q: (1) What does the bootstrap do, and when would you use it? (2) Why does the naive bootstrap fail for financial time series? (3) For AR(1) returns with $\rho=0.5$, how wrong is the naive SE of the mean? (4) What do you use instead?
pts: (1) Replace the unknown distribution by the empirical one (mass $1/n$ per observation), resample with replacement, recompute the statistic. Use it when there is no clean formula: SE of a Sharpe ratio, median, max drawdown, a difference of Sharpes.
(2) Resampling single observations assumes i.i.d.; it destroys autocorrelation and volatility clustering.
(3) True $\mathrm{Var}(\bar r)\approx\frac{\sigma^2}{n}\frac{1+\rho}{1-\rho}=3\frac{\sigma^2}{n}$, so the naive SE is $\sqrt{1/3}\approx58\%$ of the truth.
(4) Moving-block or stationary bootstrap with blocks longer than the dependence; for panels resample whole dates.

cards.q: Panel of returns $r_{it}$ for assets $i$ and periods $t$. (1) Write the time-series regression and interpret its coefficients. (2) Write the cross-sectional regression and interpret its slope. (3) What portfolio is the cross-sectional slope? (4) Summarise the difference in one line each.
pts: (1) For each asset: $$r_{it}=\alpha_i+\beta_i^\top f_t+\varepsilon_{it}$$ $\beta_i$ = exposure, $\alpha_i$ = pricing error; natural when factors are traded returns (Fama-French).
(2) For each date: $$r_{it}=\gamma_{0t}+\lambda_t^\top z_{it}+u_{it}$$ $\lambda_t$ = return earned per unit of characteristic that period (factor premium).
(3) $\hat\lambda_t=\sum_i w_i r_{it}$ with $w_i=\frac{z_i-\bar z}{\sum_j(z_j-\bar z)^2}$: a long-short portfolio with weights proportional to the demeaned characteristic.
(4) Time series: how sensitive is this asset to the factor? Cross-section: do high-characteristic stocks earn more? Fama-MacBeth runs the cross-section each period and averages.

cards.q: (1) Describe the two Fama-MacBeth steps and the standard error. (2) What does it handle automatically? (3) What problem arises when $\hat\lambda_t$ is autocorrelated? (4) What problems arise when the regressors are estimated betas, or firms have persistent effects?
pts: (1) Each period, cross-sectional regression → $\hat\lambda_t$. Then $\bar\lambda=\frac1T\sum_t\hat\lambda_t$ with SE $=s(\hat\lambda_t)/\sqrt T$.
(2) Same-period cross-sectional correlation: it lives inside each $\hat\lambda_t$. Pooled OLS treating $NT$ observations as independent can overstate $t$ several-fold.
(3) Persistent characteristics or overlapping returns make the simple SE too small: use Newey-West on the $\hat\lambda_t$ series.

(4) Errors-in-variables: estimated betas bias $\lambda$ toward zero and the SE ignores first-stage noise (Shanken correction, portfolio betas). Persistent firm effects are not handled: cluster by firm.

cards.q: Two models A and B produce $h$-step forecasts with errors $e_{A,t}, e_{B,t}$. (1) What do you fix first? (2) Why work with paired loss differentials? (3) Write the DM statistic and say why it needs HAC. (4) What complications remain?
pts: (1) The loss (MSE, MAE, or one tied to use: rank IC, portfolio P&L), and genuinely OOS forecasts from both models on the same rolling or expanding windows.
(2) $d_t=L(e_{A,t})-L(e_{B,t})$: pairing cancels the shocks both models face.
(3) $$DM=\frac{\bar d}{\sqrt{\widehat{\mathrm{LRV}}(d_t)/T}}\ \approx N(0,1)$$ $h$-step forecasts make $d_t$ at least MA($h-1$), so the long-run variance needs HAC.

(4) Nested models distort DM's null (use Clark-West); tuning on validation data adds uncertainty; many models need a model confidence set or White's reality check / SPA. In practice: test the difference of two IC series with Newey-West.
